articles.title: Photoshop’s new AI Assisted Editor offers a prompt-based editing option
articles.description: Adobe has added a simplified editing mode to Photoshop designed to help new users get acquainted with the popular image editing app. AI Assisted Editor, now available in beta, is an optional alternative to the standard view — now called Pro Editor mode — that provides a prompt-based interface similar to the Firefly editor rather than the full range of Photoshop tools. It includes a side panel that contains generative AI (genAI) features such as Generative Fill, Remove Background, and AI Markup, as well as a text prompt box. The more streamlined editor view could also prove useful for existing users that don’t need the full workspace for every edit, Adobe said. More seasoned professionals might switch to the AI Assisted Editor for concepts or mock ups, or for quick editing that doesn’t require the full set of Photoshop functions. For those who don’t need it, however, the new mode can be hidden from view. Among the other Photoshop features unveiled Thursday is Prompt to Edit, which lets users apply changes to an entire image with a simple prompt — for example, adding stormy clouds and rain. That creates an output layer that can then be modified, such as masking out image elements or changing the opacity. Prompt to Edit is available in both AI Assisted and Pro Editor views. A new “markup” feature lets users “visually communicate” edits to Firefly by drawing onto an image, indicating areas to recolor, for instance. This makes it easier to direct the AI model compared to text prompts. The Instruct Edit with Masks, which relies on Firefly Image 5, lets users specify what elements of an image to change with text prompts, with unmasked areas left untouched. Other updates include Light Adjustment Layer, which provides “professional-grade” lighting controls, such as exposure, contrast and shadows, in a non-destructive adjustment layer, Adobe said. A Stock Panel integration provides access to more than 900 million Adobe Stock assets in Photoshop via a dockable panel, while another addition, Dynamic Text, Shapes and Paths, automatically adapts text along curves as freeform layouts.

articles.title: 3 Gmail features that save you from embarrassing email mistakes
articles.description: Gmail has a few handy tools that give you more control over when your emails go out, and what happens after you hit the send button. Here are my favorites: Schedule send I don’t know about you, but there are plenty of times when I want to write an email now and don’t want it landing in someone’s inbox until later. Sometimes I’m working late, I want to draft a birthday message while I still remember, or I’m trying not to bother a coworker while they’re on vacation. Gmail’s Schedule send feature makes this easy. Simply write your email like normal, then click the small arrow next to the Send button, and choose Schedule send . Gmail offers a few suggested times, or you can pick your own date and time instead. You can also find scheduled messages in the Scheduled folder below your Inbox, where you can cancel or edit them before they go out. Gmail lets you queue up to 100 scheduled emails. Undo send Another nifty feature most people overlook is the Undo Send option. Despite its name, it doesn’t actually take a sent email back after it reaches someone’s inbox. Instead, it allows you a second chance to make any corrections before sending the email. After you send an email, a small black box appears at the bottom of your window with the option to click Undo . By default , Gmail is set to wait a short time before actually sending your emails. You can change that delay to five, 10, 20, or 30 seconds under Settings. Hit Undo during that window and the message pops back into your draft without ever being sent. Once the hidden timer runs out, though, it’s sent for good. Confidential mode Then there’s Confidential mode , which serves a different purpose. It lets you set an expiration date, revoke access, require a passcode, and block built-in options for forwarding, copying, printing, or downloading a message. To turn it on, click on the lock icon at the bottom of your Gmail messaging window. Here you can set the expiration date and require a passcode. All emails that have Confidential mode enabled will automatically restrict forwarding, copying, printing, or downloading. Just don’t mistake it for foolproof security—there are always ways around these types of protections. Someone can still take a screenshot or photo of what you sent, for example.
